title: Web scraping
summary: Read bike station web pages with rvest. Select elements, extract text and attributes, build a table from station cards, and read an HTML table.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse), library(rvest)

runs.purpose: load rvest, which reads data from web pages

steps.explain: rvest reads HTML, the language web pages are written in, and finds things in it. The lab has no internet, so these pages are copies in `data/site`; the code is the same for a page on the web, given its URL.

steps.title: Read a page: read_html()

runs.task: Read `data/site/stations.html` with `read_html()` and store it in `page`.

steps.explain:
HTML marks up a page with elements: a start tag such as `

`, content, and an end tag, `

`. Elements nest, and a start tag can carry attributes, such as `class="station"` or `href="…"`. `read_html()` parses the page, and `html_elements()` finds every element matching a CSS selector; the simplest selector is a tag's name, `h1`. To see the markup, click `stations.html` in the Files pane and choose Open in Editor.

steps.title: CSS selectors: the station cards

runs.purpose: find every station card, an `article` with the class `station`, as `cards`
runs.task: Find the `article` elements with class `station` (`"article.station"`), and store them in `cards`.

runs.purpose: take each card's name as text
runs.task: From each card, take the element with class `name` (`".name"`) with `html_element()`, then its text with `html_text2()`.

steps.explain: In a CSS selector, `.station` means "with the class station", so `article.station` picks the {n_cards} station cards and nothing else on the page. `html_element()`, singular, finds one element inside each card: its name. `html_text2()` takes the text out of the tags, the way a browser would show it, so `&` becomes &.

steps.title: Attributes: html_attr()

runs.purpose: take each card's link to the station's page
runs.task: From each card, take the `a` element with class `details`, then its `href` attribute with `html_attr()`.

steps.explain: A link's text is just Details; where it leads is in its `href` attribute. `html_attr()` reads an attribute's value, here each station's page, `station.html?id=…`, which holds the station's ID. A scraper that follows links reads these, then reads each page they lead to.

steps.title: One row per card: missing fields

runs.purpose: find every note on any card, with `html_elements()`
runs.task: Find every element with class `note` in `cards` with `html_elements()`, plural, and take their text.

runs.code:
stations <- tibble(
  name = cards |> html_element(".name") |> html_text2(),
  docks = cards |> html_element(".count") |> html_text2() |> parse_integer(),
  note = cards |> html_element(".note") |> html_text2()
)
alternatives: stations = tibble(name = html_text2(html_element(cards, '.name')), docks = parse_integer(html_text2(html_element(cards, '.count'))), note = html_text2(html_element(cards, '.note')))
runs.purpose: build a table with one row per card: its name, docks and note, as `stations`
runs.task: Make a tibble `stations` with one row per card. Use `html_element()` for `.name` text, `.count` text as a whole number with `parse_integer()`, and `.note` text.

runs.purpose: show the stations that have a note
runs.task: Keep the rows of `stations` that have a `note`.

steps.explain:
Only {n_notes} cards have a note, so `html_elements()` returns {n_notes} notes with no way of telling which card each belongs to. `html_element()`, singular, returns exactly one result for each card, `NA` where the card has no note, so every column of `stations` lines up, row by row, with the cards.

Always select the repeated unit first, here the cards, then one element inside each.

steps.title: Tables: html_table()

runs.purpose: read the fares page's table straight into a tibble
runs.task: Read `data/site/fares.html`, find its `table` element and turn it into a tibble with `html_table()`.

steps.explain:
An HTML table already has rows and columns, so `html_table()` turns it into a tibble in one step, with the header row as column names. The prices are text, such as $1.50, for `parse_number()` to turn into numbers.

Before scraping a real site, read its terms of use and its `robots.txt`, keep your requests slow, and don't collect personal data; if the site offers a download or an API, use that instead.
